2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious risk — Out of 3,922 enrolled households (1,969 CWS and 1,953 IWS), Round 2 regression models excluded 30.2% of observations for ongoing expenditures (n = 2,739), 31.5% for total monetary costs (n = 2,688), 21.5% for time spent (n = 3,078), and 12.0% for amortized investment (n = 3,453), while billed-volume analyses suffered severe differential missingness across IWS versus CWS zones and lower wealth quintiles due to unmetered connections and unavailable utility bills, without missing-data adjustment or a round-by-round attrition flow table.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Moderate risk — Eight CWS demonstration wards were non-randomly selected for ease of hydraulic isolation and household-level pre-2008 baseline outcomes were unavailable, but the authors mitigated observable confounding via ward-level genetic matching on a pre-intervention 2006 survey of 15,000 households (matching on SES, household tap/latrine access, garbage collection, pre-CWS delivery frequency, and health spending) combined with household-level SES covariate regressions.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: High — Municipal water service rules, administrative ward boundaries, and tariff reforms under KUWASIP versus status-quo Hubli-Dharwad Municipal Corporation intermittent supply are precisely specified, including universal connection registration, metering charges, flat versus volumetric increasing block tariffs (Rs/kL tiers), decommissioning of free public standpipes and borewells, and World Bank/WSP project finance categories.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk — Enumerators and respondents could not be blinded to neighborhood CWS versus IWS status; monthly waiting/collection time relied on subjective recall despite respondents multitasking on household chores while waiting; and water bill and volumetric consumption measurement differed systematically across arms because CWS connections were universally metered whereas many IWS and low-SES/tenant households lacked meters or utility bills (and informal side payments in IWS zones were excluded).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Durable household infrastructure and storage investments were anchored by physical inspections, a 707-household container measurement subsample, and local retail market price surveys, but primary time-savings and income measures relied on unblinded recall, volumetric consumption relied on partial metered bills differentially missing in IWS and poorer households, and utility-level NPV relied on inconsistent secondary World Bank/WSP cost reports.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate risk — No pre-registered protocol or economic pre-analysis plan is cited; Section 4 regressions report Round 2 out of 4 survey rounds (whereas Section 5 NPV equations average across rounds) and collected medical expenses and illness-care time were omitted due to small/undetectable differences, although extensive sensitivity checks across covariates, five utility cost assumptions, and wage-time valuations are transparently reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk — Households were enrolled in November 2010–February 2012, roughly 2–4 years after the 2008 CWS pilot rollout rather than at intervention inception, using systematic landmark-walk sampling restricted to households with a child under age 5 (n = 1,969 CWS; n = 1,953 IWS), without reporting refusal/non-response rates across arms or testing for post-2008 residential mobility.

domain_ratings.justification: Eight of 67 municipal wards were purposively chosen for the 2008 CWS pilot based on ease of hydraulic isolation within the piped network, and no pre-2008 household-level baseline data on water expenditures, meter coverage, or water usage existed for enrolled households. However, the authors applied multivariate genetic matching using a pre-intervention 15,000-household survey (CMDR, 2006) to match eight control IWS wards on ward-level economic indicators, female illiteracy, tap/latrine presence, garbage collection, pre-CWS water delivery frequency, and pre-intervention health expenditures, and controlled for household-level SES proxies in OLS regressions (though the PCA wealth index used post-upgrade assets/materials and regressions did not report ward-clustered standard errors). Residual ward/hydraulic-level confounding remains possible but observable confounding was rigorously addressed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Participant recruitment occurred in November 2010–February 2012, 2–4 years after CWS implementation began in 2008, creating a prevalent-exposure cohort rather than an inception cohort at intervention start (meaning post-2008 residential sorting cannot be wholly excluded). Within matched wards, systematic landmark-walk sampling enrolled ~250 households per ward restricted to families with a child under age 5 (applied identically in both CWS and IWS arms), but household refusal and non-response rates by arm were not reported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Within CWS wards, about half of households experienced at least one brief service interruption (42% lasting 1–6 hours) over 15 months, which reflects real-world operational performance of the reform. However, in the control IWS wards, the municipal utility made concurrent network investments during the 2010–2012 study window that temporarily altered intermittent delivery frequencies (before later reverting to once weekly or less), introducing modest co-intervention variation in the comparator arm during follow-up.

domain_ratings.justification: Out of 3,922 enrolled households (1,969 CWS and 1,953 IWS), primary Round 2 regression models in Table 4 show substantial complete-case attrition/missingness: 30.2% missing for ongoing expenditures (n = 2,739), 31.5% missing for total monetary costs (n = 2,688), 21.5% missing for monthly time (n = 3,078), and 12.0% missing for amortized investments (n = 3,453), with no missingness breakdown by arm or statistical adjustment (such as IPW or multiple imputation). Furthermore, billed water volume data (Fig. 5) were available only for households with both a meter and a reported/shown bill, resulting in pronounced differential missingness across both intervention arms (many IWS households lacked meters whereas CWS connections were universally metered) and socio-economic strata (lowest wealth quintile and tenants). Small-container costs were also imputed from a 707-household subsample.

domain_ratings.justification: Neither respondents nor enumerators were blinded to CWS versus IWS status in a politically contested pilot reform. Monthly hours spent waiting for, collecting, and treating water—the primary driver of positive household net economic benefits—relied on subjective respondent recall even though respondents simultaneously performed other chores while waiting. Moreover, measurement of water bills and volumetric consumption was not comparable in reliability across arms and SES strata: CWS connections were universally metered and billed by the utility, whereas IWS and low-SES households frequently lacked meters or paid landlords and relied on unverified recall when bills were unavailable, and informal side payments to frontline valve workers in IWS zones were omitted. Secondary utility cost inputs for NPV also suffered from inconsistent World Bank/WSP reporting, though household durable asset values were carefully cross-checked against physical inspections and a local market price survey.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-registered study protocol or pre-analysis plan for the economic evaluation is cited. The authors report post-hoc analytical choices—specifically presenting Round 2 data alone for most Section 4 household analyses (stating in Footnote 6 that robustness checks across all four rounds yielded similar results, while averaging all rounds in Section 5 NPV equations) and excluding collected medical expenses and illness-care time because reported values were too small to yield detectable inter-arm differences. Risk is judged Moderate rather than Serious because the omission of near-zero health-care coping costs is transparently disclosed and extensive sensitivity specifications (full covariate models in SI Table S6, five project cost definitions in Table 5, and 25% vs 50% wage valuations of time in SI Tables S13–S14) are reported.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Burt et al. (2018) conduct a quasi-experimental matched-cohort and system-level cost-benefit evaluation of the World Bank-supported KUWASIP pilot upgrade from intermittent water supply (IWS) to continuous 24x7 piped water supply (CWS) in Hubli-Dharwad, India. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the overall risk of bias is Serious, driven by D5 (Bias due to missing data) and D6 (Bias in measurement of outcomes). Methodological strengths are substantial: the authors used pre-intervention data from a 15,000-household survey (CMDR, 2006) and multivariate genetic matching to pair the eight CWS wards with eight comparable IWS wards across socioeconomic, demographic, health-spending, and pre-CWS water delivery indicators; supplemented matching with household-level SES regression controls; and cross-validated household infrastructure/equipment costs using physical measurements (including a 707-household container audit) and local retail price surveys. However, major threats to internal validity remain: (1) over 30% of the 3,922 enrolled households are missing from the main Round 2 expenditure regressions (Table 4), and volumetric consumption/bill comparisons (Fig. 5) suffer from structural differential missingness because CWS universalized metering whereas many IWS and low-SES/tenant households lacked meters or utility bills (D5: Serious); (2) unblinded respondents self-reported monthly waiting hours despite multitasking during waiting, bill/volume measurement reliability differed across arms, and informal side payments in IWS wards were omitted (D6: Serious); and (3) CWS wards were purposively chosen for hydraulic isolation ease, household enrollment occurred 2–4 years post-upgrade without pre-2008 household-level baselines or ward-clustered standard errors, and no pre-analysis plan was registered (D1, D2, D4, D7: Moderate; D3: Low).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental matched-cohort longitudinal household survey (genetic matching of 8 continuous water supply pilot wards to 8 intermittent water supply control wards using pre-intervention 2006 survey data, followed by 4 post-intervention survey rounds of 3,922 households over 15 months with multivariable OLS regressions) combined with a household- and utility-level net present value (NPV) cost-benefit analysis.

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a non-randomized municipal infrastructure and tariff reform intervention (conversion from intermittent to continuous 24x7 piped water supply with universal metering, increasing block tariffs, and removal of free public taps/borewells) against a matched comparator arm (eight intermittent supply wards selected via genetic matching) using longitudinal panel surveys and econometric regression. ROBINS-I is the exact dedicated instrument for non-randomized comparative studies of policy/infrastructure interventions.
